title: Profit, Loss & Discount
relevance: Core quantitative aptitude for campus OAs; modern variants wrap the same CP/SP math in bulk cost, defect, and platform-fee stories.
company_notes: Modern OAs at Uber or Amazon often wrap simple profit equations in operational story problems (bulk purchasing, defect rates, platform fees).

phases.goal: Establish CP, SP, MP and where profit/loss vs discount percentages are taken.

must_hit.point: Cost Price is purchase price, Selling Price is sale price, Marked Price is the listed/printed price.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Names CP, SP, and MP and distinguishes purchase, sale, and list price.

must_hit.point: Profit % and Loss % are always calculated on CP: (SP−CP)/CP×100 or (CP−SP)/CP×100.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States the base is CP and writes or paraphrases both percentage formulas.

must_hit.point: Discount is always calculated on MP, with SP = MP×(1−d/100).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Says discount base is MP and gives the SP-from-MP formula.

must_hit.point: SP from CP uses SP = CP×(1±p/100) with + for profit and − for loss.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Recalls the one-step CP-to-SP scaling with signed percentage p.

probes: Define CP, SP, and MP, and state what base profit/loss % and discount % use.

hints.1: Separate purchase, sale, and list price before writing any percentage.
hints.2: Profit/loss hang off CP; discount hangs off MP.

phases.goal: Apply successive discounts, SP scaling, MP/CP linkage, and false-weight gain formulas.

must_hit.point: Successive discounts of a% and b% equal a single discount of (a+b−ab/100)%.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States the combined-discount formula and can plug a and b.

must_hit.point: Between two SPs of the same item at different profit/loss rates, SP2 = SP1×(100±p2)/(100±p1) without finding CP.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Uses the SP scaling ratio with both (100±p) factors.

must_hit.point: MP/CP = (100+Profit%)/(100−Discount%) links markup target and discount.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Writes the MP-to-CP ratio in terms of profit % and discount %.

must_hit.point: For sale-at-claimed-CP with false weight, Gain% = (Error/(True Value−Error))×100, denominator = actual weight given.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States the error-over-actual-weight gain formula and names the denominator.

probes: How do you combine two successive discounts, and how do you move between two selling prices without computing CP?

hints.1: Successive % changes are not a plain sum.
hints.2: Combine with a+b−ab/100; scale SPs with (100±p) ratios.

phases.goal: Choose ratio chaining vs explicit CP, and successive % vs adding percentages.

must_hit.point: Prefer SP scaling with (100±p) ratios over finding CP when only profit/loss rates change between two selling prices.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Says skip CP and multiply by the two (100±p) factors.

must_hit.point: Markup then discount (or claimed loss then false weight) should use successive/ratio chaining, not adding the percentages.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Rejects adding % and multiplies the step ratios instead.

must_hit.point: When cheating on both buy and sell weights, do not add the cheat percentages; bases change because more is acquired and less is delivered.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Warns against summing buy/sell cheats and cites changing bases.

probes: When would you scale selling prices directly instead of computing cost price, and when is adding percentage effects wrong?

hints.1: Ask whether the cost base is fixed or each step changes the base.
hints.2: Same-item SP change → ratio scale; chained markup/discount/weight → multiply factors.
hints.3: Use SP2 = SP1×(100±p2)/(100±p1); never add successive or dual-cheat percentages—chain ratios.

phases.goal: Solve multi-article, promotion, equal±% SP, and OA story mappings to net CP/SP.

must_hit.point: If CP of 15 articles equals SP of 12, then SP/CP = 15/12 = 5/4, so profit is 25%.
Buy 3 Get 2 Free: pay for 3 of 5 items, so discount % = 2/5×100 = 40%.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Uses free/total items for discount and gets 40%.

must_hit.point: Two items sold at the same SP with equal opposite profit/loss x% give net Loss% = x²/100, not break-even.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States the x²/100 net-loss rule and rejects no-profit-no-loss.

must_hit.point: OA stories need all costs mapped to one net CP (and sellable units or net revenue after fees) before standard profit formulas.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Mentions folding shipping, breakage, or commission into net CP/revenue first.

probes: Two houses sell for the same price with +20% and −20%; is the deal break-even, and how do OA bulk/fee stories change the setup?

hints.1: Equal opposite % on the same SP is a classic trap.
hints.2: Net loss is x²/100; promotions use free/total; story costs collapse to one CP.
hints.3: Loss% = x²/100; Buy 3 Get 2 Free → 40%; map shipping/defects/fees into net CP then apply SP formulas.

tradeoffs.topic: Explicit CP vs SP scaling ratio
tradeoffs.strong_answer: When the same item moves between two known profit/loss percentages, scale with SP2 = SP1×(100±p2)/(100±p1) instead of solving for CP first.
Successive discounts use a+b−ab/100; markup-plus-discount and false-weight stacks multiply ratios—adding the percentages misstates the net effect.

tradeoffs.topic: Claimed break-even vs net loss on equal opposite %
tradeoffs.strong_answer: Same SP with +x% and −x% is never no profit no loss; percentages sit on different CPs, so net Loss% = x²/100.

gotchas.trap: Guessing no profit no loss when two items sell at the same price with equal opposite profit and loss percentages.
gotchas.correction: There is always a net loss; Loss% = x²/100 (e.g. x = 20 gives 4% loss).

gotchas.trap: Adding cheat percentages when a dealer falsifies weights on both buying and selling.
gotchas.correction: Bases change—more goods acquired, fewer delivered—so chain the buy and sell weight ratios instead of summing the percentages.

gotchas.trap: Treating OA story extras (shipping, breakage, marketplace commission) as afterthoughts separate from CP/SP.
gotchas.correction: Fold them into a single net CP (and net revenue or sellable count) before applying standard profit formulas.
